prompt: In a versioned bucket, what does `gcloud storage rm gs://quitanda-curated-prod/customers/customers.csv`, with no generation, do on Cloud Storage?
hint: There is no delete marker in Cloud Storage.

choices.text: It removes every generation of the name
choices.why: Only deletes that name a generation remove anything for good.

choices.text: It makes the live generation noncurrent
choices.why: Right. The name stops being listed; copying a generation back restores it.

choices.text: It adds an empty delete marker on top of the live version
choices.why: That is another object store's mechanism. Cloud Storage has no marker: the name simply has no live generation.

choices.text: It is refused, because versioned objects cannot be deleted
choices.why: Versioning refuses nothing; a retention policy is what refuses deletes.

prompt: The customer table was deleted by mistake in a versioned bucket. How does Quitanda bring it back?
hint: A noncurrent generation can be the source of a copy.

choices.text: `gcloud storage restore` on the name
choices.why: That restores soft-deleted objects; a noncurrent version is not soft-deleted.

choices.text: Turn versioning off and on again
choices.why: Versioning off keeps the noncurrent versions where they are and brings nothing back.

choices.text: Copy the generation wanted onto the name
choices.why: Right: `gcloud storage cp gs://…#GENERATION gs://…` writes a new live generation with those bytes.

choices.text: Delete the newest noncurrent generation
choices.why: That destroys a version; there is no marker to remove in Cloud Storage.

prompt: Quitanda turns versioning off on a bucket that holds 40 noncurrent versions. What happens to them?
hint: Turning it off changes the next write.

choices.text: They stay, still listed and billed, until something deletes them
choices.why: Right. Off stops the growth and keeps what was kept.

choices.text: They are deleted at once
choices.why: Nothing is deleted by the setting; a rule or a delete per generation does that.

choices.text: They become soft-deleted for seven days
choices.why: Soft delete applies to deleted or replaced objects, and turning versioning off deletes nothing.

choices.text: They are merged into the live object
choices.why: Generations are separate objects; nothing merges them.

prompt: A second, separate protection that Google turns on for new buckets keeps a deleted or replaced object for seven days by default. It is called soft ___.
hint: `gcloud storage restore` brings its objects back.

prompt: A 20 GiB file is rewritten every night in a versioned bucket with no rule, in Standard at 0.035 USD per GiB-month. How many GiB does the bucket hold after 100 nights?
hint: Every night adds one full copy.

prompt: Versioning is off on Quitanda's curated bucket, and its 50 GiB table is rewritten nightly. Why does the bucket hold 400 GiB?
hint: Something keeps replaced objects whether you asked or not.

choices.text: Noncurrent versions are kept anyway, versioning or not
choices.why: With versioning off there are no noncurrent versions of new writes.

choices.text: Soft delete keeps each old copy a week
choices.why: Right: the live table plus seven soft-deleted ones, billed at the class's price.

choices.text: The emulator miscounts
choices.why: The number comes from the program's arithmetic, which models Cloud Storage.

choices.text: A rewrite is billed as two copies
choices.why: A rewrite is one Class A operation; it does not double the storage.

prompt: A versioned bucket deletes noncurrent versions 7 days after they are replaced, and soft delete is on at 7 days. A 50 GiB table is rewritten nightly. What is the most the bucket is billed for?
hint: Count the live one, the noncurrent ones, and what happens to a version the rule deletes.

choices.text: 400 GiB: one live and seven noncurrent
choices.why: That forgets that a version the rule deletes is soft-deleted for seven more days.

choices.text: 750 GiB, fifteen copies
choices.why: Right: one live, seven noncurrent and seven soft-deleted, which is what keep.py's second column reaches.

choices.text: 50 GiB, since the rule removes old versions
choices.why: The rule waits seven days, and soft delete keeps what it removes.

choices.text: 18,000 GiB by the end of the year
choices.why: That is the bucket with no rule at all.

prompt: Match each life-cycle condition to what it tests.
hint: Some conditions only make sense in a versioned bucket.

pairs.right: Days since the object was created
Days since the version was replaced
How many newer versions of the name exist

prompt: What did fake-gcs-server do with `gcloud storage buckets update --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json`?
hint: Read the `describe` that followed.

choices.text: It applied the rules at once, since it has no clock
choices.why: It applied nothing, and kept nothing to apply.

choices.text: It refused the file as invalid
choices.why: It answered with success.

choices.text: It stored the rules and will apply them within a day
choices.why: No lifecycle_config came back from describe.

choices.text: It accepted the request and stored no rules
choices.why: Right: success, and the bucket came back with no life-cycle configuration at all.

prompt: A rule file names an action `Teleport` and, in another rule, a condition `agee`. Which does `gcloud` refuse before sending anything?
hint: The command line knows the names of one of the two.

choices.text: Both
choices.why: It passed the action type through; only the condition was checked.

choices.text: Only the misspelt condition
choices.why: Right. The action reached the emulator, which accepted it; Cloud Storage would refuse it.

choices.text: Only the unknown action
choices.why: It is the other way round in the transcript.

choices.text: Neither: gcloud checks only that the file is JSON
choices.why: It refused `agee` with an error about the lifecycle rule.

prompt: Under Quitanda's rules a GiB costs 0.4773 USD over seven years, and 2.9808 if left in Standard. For 3,000 GiB of exports, how many USD does the rule save over the seven years?
hint: Save per GiB, times the volume.

prompt: Quitanda's archive bucket has an unlocked retention policy of five years. Who can delete a three-month-old invoice in it?
hint: Unlocked policies can be changed.

choices.text: Nobody, until the five years pass
choices.why: That is true only once the policy is locked.

choices.text: Anyone with `storage.objects.delete`
choices.why: The policy refuses that delete whatever the role, while it is in place.

choices.text: An administrator, after first removing that setting
choices.why: Right: `--clear-retention-period`, then the delete. Locking is what closes that path.

choices.text: Only Google support, after a request from the project's owner
choices.why: Google support plays no part in it; an unlocked policy is the project's own to change.

prompt: A supplier contract must be kept five years after the contract ends, and nobody knows today when that will be. Which tool fits?
hint: One kind of hold moves the start of the retention clock.

choices.text: A temporary hold
choices.why: It keeps the object while it is on, and does nothing to the retention clock.

choices.text: A locked retention policy of five years
choices.why: The period would count from when the file was written, not from when the contract ends.

choices.text: Soft delete set to 90 days
choices.why: Ninety days is the longest soft delete there is, and it only starts at a deletion.

choices.text: An event-based hold
choices.why: Right. Released when the contract ends, it starts the retention period from that day.

prompt: Right after `--retention-period=1y`, `gcloud storage buckets update --lock-retention-period` failed in the lab. What does that failure show?
hint: The command line reads the policy before locking it.

choices.text: That locking needs a second person's approval
choices.why: Nothing in the command asks for one; the message was about the policy.

choices.text: That the emulator kept no policy
choices.why: Right: gcloud found no policy to lock, one command after setting it.

choices.text: That a lock can only be applied a day after the policy
choices.why: No such delay exists; the bucket simply had no policy.

choices.text: That the bucket already had a locked policy
choices.why: It had none at all, locked or not.

prompt: Why does `gcloud storage ls -a` show only the live generation against fake-gcs-server?
hint: Compare the two curl requests.

choices.text: The emulator keeps no noncurrent versions
choices.why: It keeps them: versions.py and curl with versions=true list them.

choices.text: gcloud asks with versions=True, in capitals
choices.why: Right. The emulator only understands versions=true; one letter of case decides between one generation and three.

choices.text: `-a` lists only live objects on Cloud Storage too
choices.why: On Cloud Storage `ls -a` lists every generation.

choices.text: Versioning was off when they were written
choices.why: It was on, and the noncurrent versions exist.

prompt: A pruning script deletes old generations with `gcloud storage rm gs://…#GENERATION` and passes its tests against fake-gcs-server. What did the lab show would happen in those tests?
hint: Look at the listing after the delete.

choices.text: The named generation goes and the live one stays, as on Cloud Storage
choices.why: The named generation was still listed afterwards.

choices.text: Nothing is deleted, because the emulator ignores deletes
choices.why: Something was deleted: the live version.

choices.text: The live version goes; the named one stays
choices.why: Right. A test that only checks that something went would pass while the current data disappeared.

choices.text: Every generation of the name is deleted
choices.why: The two noncurrent ones were still there.

prompt: Order the life of an export under Quitanda's rules, from when it is written.
hint: Standard first, gone last.
items: Nearline until it is a year old

prompt: Match each Quitanda need to the protection that meets it.
hint: Ask whether the threat is an accident or somebody who means it.

pairs.left: Undo last night's broken rewrite of the customer table
Keep invoices five years, even against an administrator
Keep one customer's orders until a court case ends
Recover a file deleted by mistake in an unversioned bucket

prompt: Against fake-gcs-server, a test creates a bucket with a one-year retention policy, writes an object, tries to delete it and expects a refusal. What happens?
hint: Recall what the emulator kept of the policy.

choices.text: The delete is refused, as on Cloud Storage
choices.why: The emulator kept no policy, so nothing refused it.

choices.text: The bucket creation fails
choices.why: It succeeded; the period was dropped silently.

choices.text: The delete succeeds, and the test fails
choices.why: Right, though the policy is fine on Cloud Storage. Here the emulator fails a correct test; the next mistake may be one it passes.

choices.text: The object is soft-deleted instead
choices.why: The emulator keeps no soft-deleted objects either.

prompt: Which check caught the emulator serving the wrong bytes for an old generation?
hint: It is done on every download by the command line.

choices.text: The emulator's own error message
choices.why: The emulator answered as if all was well.

choices.text: The sizes that versions.py prints
choices.why: versions.py listed the generations correctly; it reads no bytes.

choices.text: The MD5 hash gcloud checks
choices.why: Right: the bytes received did not match the hash the metadata declared.

choices.text: A retention policy
choices.why: Retention has nothing to say about which bytes are served.
